transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

I guess what brought me in is… I just don’t feel like myself anymore. It’s hard to explain without sounding like I’m just tired or being lazy, but it’s more than that. I barely talk to people now, even people I see all the time. I’ll be at work doing the cleaning route, and someone says something to me, and I just kind of go flat and quiet. Like there’s nothing in me to answer with.

And getting started on things has gotten really hard. Even the cleaning route, which I’ve done over and over, feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill before I even touch the cart. I stand there knowing what needs to be done, but it takes so much effort to make myself move. I don’t feel like I’m acting like me. That’s why I came in.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… a while. I’d say about a year and five months now, give or take. It really started building after I had to leave my old apartment and the neighborhood I knew. At first I thought maybe I was just unsettled from the move, you know, like anyone would be thrown off if they had to leave a place they were used to. But it didn’t settle down.

It’s like since then, month by month, I’ve felt less like myself. I can kind of mark it from that time because before that I wasn’t exactly perfect, but I still had my routines and places I knew, people I’d see. After leaving there, things just started to feel heavier, and it’s been going on ever since.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in things you used to enjoy or that you’ve lost interest in activities you used to like?

Yeah… yeah, I have. That’s actually one of the things that bothers me the most, because I can remember pretty clearly what I used to look forward to, and now it’s like those same things are just sitting there with no pull to them.

I used to really like fishing on Saturdays. Not even always catching anything, just getting up, getting my stuff together, being outside, having that quiet. It gave me something to aim for at the end of the week. Now Saturday comes and I’ll think, “I could go,” but then I just don’t. The gear can be right there and I still let it sit.

Same with crosswords. I used to do them with coffee, take my time with it, feel kind of pleased when I got a hard one. Now I’ll look at the puzzle and it just feels like paper. I don’t get that little bit of enjoyment from it.

Even at work, I used to like showing the younger guys tricks, like how to strip a floor without making a mess of it, little things you only learn from doing it a long time. I used to take some pride in that. Now I mostly keep to myself. It’s not that I hate those things exactly… they just don’t give me anything back anymore.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, and do you also find that you have very little energy or motivation for even small tasks?

Yeah… the energy part, definitely. It’s like even if I sleep through the night, I don’t feel like I’ve got anything in the tank when I get up. By the time I get to the building, before I’ve even really done much, my arms and legs already feel heavy, like I’ve been carrying something around all morning.

And the small jobs feel bigger than they should. Hauling trash bags, for example — I’ve done that kind of work for years, it’s not new to me. But lately I’ll grab a couple bags and it wears me out in a way that doesn’t seem right. I have to kind of talk myself through it, like, “Just get this one to the bin, then do the next thing.” It’s not that I don’t know how to do it or that the work changed. It’s more like my body and my motivation both just run out way too fast.
Have you found yourself feeling like you’re not worth much or that you’re failing at things, even when others might not see it that way?

Yeah… I do. More than I probably say out loud. It’s this feeling like I’ve let everybody down, even when I can’t exactly prove that’s true.

A lot of it goes back to losing my old place. I keep turning that over in my head like, “If I had done this different, if I had kept things together better, maybe I wouldn’t have had to leave.” And then it turns into this bigger thing, like I didn’t just lose an apartment — I failed at keeping my life steady. Like a man my age should have been able to hold onto that, you know?

And then it spreads into things that probably don’t even make sense. Like if the church pantry is short on supplies, I’ll catch myself thinking I should’ve done more, I should’ve noticed, I should’ve helped fix it somehow. Or at work, if a hallway gets missed or something isn’t cleaned the way it should be, even if it wasn’t really all on me, I feel it like it is. Like somehow I’m responsible for the whole building, the whole pantry, everybody being okay.

I know other people might say, “That’s not your fault,” and maybe part of me understands that. But it doesn’t feel that way inside. It feels like I’m always coming up short.
